doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Race, education and the future of jazz
title: Teachers, students' busy schedules and the future audience
summary: Rowe and Pug discuss academics' wariness and encouraging teachers; students' time is crowded but could become audience.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You said it pretty well. You really did. I think sometimes academics may be threatened by people who have made their living playing the music instead of just teaching about it. That that may be a threat to them. But there are some inroads being made in that.

I’d like to think so. And there are certainly teachers, I mean there’s one particular teacher at the University of New Hampshire who is very encouraging and is always getting people like Clark Terry and Bob to go up there and bring his charts and to work with them. And I think that this is one thing that you can do. You can certainly set aside some time. And I think another problem that is part of our society, Monk, is that students are being called upon to give far too many hours for other extracurricular things. That their time is so valuable. I know when Bob is doing other academic programs he would say, “Did you listen to the music? Did you play the music?” They said we haven’t had time, we had to do so-and-so, we had to do something else and so on. So I do think that our young people today are being challenged in many ways, and they’re having to prioritize. And this is not necessarily something that they’re going to go in for. Maybe they’re not going to be full time professional jazz musicians, but they could be full time professional musicians or teachers.
And they could be a great audience too.
